Surah "Tabbat" (Surah 111), which is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars). It has five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ (1)

There are three issues here.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﹘﴾. It is related in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, the Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere, and the wording is Muslim's, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the verse ﴿And warn your closest kindred﹘﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:214] and ﴿and your family among them, the sincere ones﹘﴾ was revealed, (1) the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out until he climbed al-Safa and shouted, "Yaa sabaahaah!" (2) They said, "Who is this calling out?" They said, "Muhammad." So they gathered around him. He said, "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so, O Banu 'Abd Manaf, O Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib!" So they gathered around him, and he said, "Tell me, if I informed you that cavalry were coming out at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said, "We have never found you to be a liar." He said, "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said, "Perish you! Did you gather us only for this?" Then he got up, and this surah was revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he﹘﴾ to the end of the surah. Al-A'mash recited it this way.

Al-Humaydi and others added: When his wife heard what had been revealed about her husband, and the Qur'an in it, she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was sitting in the mosque near the Ka'bah, with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) beside him. In her hand was a fahr (a stone the size of a palm, and it is said any stone at all) (3). When she stood before him, Allah took her sight away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so she could see only Abu Bakr. She said, "O Abu Bakr, your companion has reached me, claiming that he satirizes me. By Allah, if I found him I would strike his mouth with this stone. By Allah, I am a poetess:

We have disobeyed Mudhammam,
We have rejected his command,
And we have abandoned his religion."

Then she left. Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah, did she not see you?" He said, "She did not see me. Allah took her sight away from me." The Quraysh used to call the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "Mudhammam" and revile him, but he would say, "Do you not wonder how Allah has turned away from me the harm of the Quraysh? They revile and satirize Mudhammam, while I am Muhammad."

It is also said that the occasion of revelation was what 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd related: Abu Lahab came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "What will I be given if I believe in you, O Muhammad?" He said, "What the Muslims are given." He said, "Do I have no superiority over them?" He said, "And what do you seek?" He said, "Perish this religion! That I should be equal to these people!" So Allah, exalted is He, revealed about him: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he﹘﴾.

A third view, related by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Kaysan, is that whenever a delegation came to the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Lahab would go out to them, and they would ask him about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, "You know him better than we do." Abu Lahab would tell them, "He is a liar and a sorcerer." So they would turn away from him and not meet him. Then a delegation came, and he did the same with them. They said, "We will not leave until we see him and hear his words." Abu Lahab said to them, "We have not ceased to deal with him, so perish him and ruin!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of this and was grieved, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﹘﴾ to the end of the surah.

It is also said that Abu Lahab wanted to strike the Prophet (ﷺ) with a stone, but Allah prevented him, and Allah revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he﹘﴾, as a reply to the restraint that befell him.

The meaning of "tabbat" is "lost", according to Qatadah. It is said it means "failed", according to Ibn 'Abbas. It is said it means "went astray", according to 'Ata'. It is said it means "destroyed", according to Ibn Jubayr. Yaman ibn Ri'ab said: "emptied of all good news."

Al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that when 'Uthman (may Allah have mercy on him) was killed, people heard a voice calling:

"They have forsaken you and gone away,
Neither refusing nor returning.
They did not fulfill their pledge,
So woe to what they have done!"

The hands are singled out for the ruin (tabab) because most work is done by them, meaning: they lost, and he lost. It is also said that the hands here mean his very self. The hand is sometimes used to refer to the self, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﹘﴾ [al-Hajj 22:10], meaning: your own self. This is the clear and common way of Arabic speech, expressing a part of a thing to mean the whole. You say: "The hand of time has struck him," and "the calamities and deaths have struck him," meaning that all of that befell him. The poet said:

"When the hand of calamities fell upon him,
He called out: 'Is there no protector?'"

As for "watabba": al-Farra' said, "The first tabb is a supplication and the second is a statement, as one says: 'May Allah destroy him,' and 'He has been destroyed.'" In the recitation of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy (ibn Ka'b) it is "wa-qad tabba" (and he has indeed perished).

Abu Lahab's name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, and he was the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib, the paternal uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). His wife was al-'Awraa' Umm Jamil, the sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. Both of them were extremely hostile to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Tariq ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muharibi said: "I was in the market of Dhu al-Majaz when I saw a man saying, 'O people, say: There is no god but Allah, and you will prosper.' Behind him was a man pelting him, who had drawn blood from his shins and heels, and he was saying, 'O people, he is a liar, so do not believe him.' I asked, 'Who is this?' They said, 'Muhammad, who claims to be a prophet. And this is his paternal uncle Abu Lahab, who claims he is a liar.'"

'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that Abu Lahab said, "Muhammad has bewitched you! Indeed one of us eats a young goat (al-ju'dha, a kid in its second year) and drinks a large cup (al-'us, a big bowl) of milk and is not satisfied, while Muhammad has satisfied you with a thigh of sheep and given you milk to drink from a large bowl."

The second issue concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Abi Lahab﹘﴾. It is said he was named "Lahab" (flame) for his beauty and the brightness of his face. Some people have thought that this is evidence for giving a kunyah (honorific nickname such as "father of") to a polytheist, but this is false. According to the scholars, Allah called him "Abu Lahab" for four reasons:

First: his name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, and al-'Uzza is an idol, and Allah does not attribute worship to an idol in His Book.

Second: he was better known by his kunyah than by his name, so He named him by it.

Third: the name is more noble than the kunyah, so Allah, mighty and majestic is He, lowered him from the more noble to the less noble, since it was unavoidable to speak of him. This is why Allah called the prophets by their names and did not give any of them a kunyah. What shows the nobility of the name over the kunyah is that Allah, exalted is He, is named but is not given a kunyah, even though this would be for His manifestation and clarity, and attributing a kunyah to Him is impossible, since He is exalted above it.

Fourth: Allah, exalted is He, willed to confirm his lineage by causing him to enter the Fire, so that he would be "father of it" (the Fire), a confirmation of the name and a fulfilment of the omen and the ill-omen that He chose for him. It has also been said that his name was his kunyah: his family called him "Abu Lahab" because of the blaze of his face and his beauty. So Allah turned them away from saying "Abu al-Nur" (father of light) and "Abu al-Diya'" (father of radiance), which are shared between what is loved and what is hated, and caused their tongues to attach him to "Lahab" (flame), which is specific to what is hated and blameworthy, namely the Fire. Then He confirmed this by making the Fire his dwelling place.

Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin recited "Abi Lahb" with the h sukun (sukun on the ha'). They did not differ regarding "dhata lahab" (﹘﹘ "a flame of fire"), which is with a fathah, because they observed the verse-endings (ru'us al-ay, the rhyme at the ends of verses).

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas said, "When Allah, mighty and majestic, created the Pen, He said to it, 'Write what is to be.' Among what it wrote was: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﹘﴾." Mansur said: Al-Hasan was asked about His saying, ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﹘﴾: "Was this in Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book)? And was it possible for Abu Lahab not to burn in the Fire?" He said, "By Allah, he could not avoid burning in it, and it is indeed in the Book of Allah before Abu Lahab and his parents were created." This is supported by the statement of Musa to Adam: "You are the one whom Allah created with His hand, breathed into you from His spirit, made dwell in His Garden, and commanded His angels to prostrate to you. You caused people to err and expelled them from the Garden." Adam said, "And you are Musa, whom Allah chose with His speech and gave the Torah. Do you blame me for a matter that Allah wrote for me before He created the heavens and the earth?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So Adam overcame Musa in argument" (fahajja Adamu Musa) (4). This has been mentioned before (5).

In the hadith of Hammam from Abu Hurayrah, Adam said to Musa, "How long before creating me did Allah write the Torah?" He said, "Two thousand years." He said, "Did you find in it: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﹘﴾?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Do you blame me for a matter that Allah wrote for me to do before I was created, by two thousand years?" So Adam overcame (hajja) Musa (6) in argument.

In the hadith of Tawus, Ibn Hurmuz and al-A'raj from Abu Hurayrah: "by forty years."

---

Notes:
1. Qur'an 26:214–215.
2. A cry used to raise an alarm in danger.
3. Fahr: a stone that fills the palm; some say any stone.
4. Lit. "defeated him by argument."
5. Refers to an earlier passage in the commentary (vol. 11, p. 256).
6. Lit. "overcame him by the strength of his argument."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 111, verse 2:

﴿مَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ﴾ (2)

That is: what he had gathered of wealth did not avert from him the punishment of Allah, nor did what he earned of status (jah). Mujahid said: "[It refers to] his offspring, and a man's offspring is part of his earnings."

Al-A'mash recited "وَمَا اكْتَسَبَ" (wa-ma iktasaba, "and what he acquired"), and he related it from Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Tufayl said: The sons of Abu Lahab came disputing before Ibn Abbas, and they came to blows. He rose to separate them, but one of them pushed him, and he fell upon the bedding. Ibn Abbas became angry and said: "Remove from me the evil earnings," meaning his son.

On the authority of Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed my children are from his earnings." Abu Dawud related it.

Ibn Abbas said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) warned his kinsfolk of the Fire, Abu Lahab said: "If what my nephew says is true, then I will ransom myself with my wealth and my children." So there was revealed: ﴿مَا أَغْنَى عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ﴾.

Regarding "مَا" in His words "مَا أَغْنَى": it may be a negation, and it may be an interrogative, meaning "What benefited him?" As for the second "مَا": it may mean "الَّذِي" (alladhi, "that which"), and it may be, together with the verb, a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: his wealth and his earning did not benefit him.

[مأي] ذَاتَ اشْتِعَالٍ وَتَلَهُّبٍ. [...blazing and flaming fire.] The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-Mursalat (see vol. 19, p. 160).

The common reading (al-qira'ah al-ʿammah) is *sayaṣlā* with a fatḥah on the yā'. Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read it with a ḍammah on the yā' (*sayuṣlā*). This reading is also transmitted from Mahbub, from Isma'il, from Ibn Kathir, and from Husayn, from Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, and it is reported from al-Hasan. Ashhab al-ʿUqayli, Abu Sammal al-ʿAdawi, and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read *sayuṣallā* with a ḍammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ṣād, and a shaddah on the lām. Its meaning is "Allah will cause him to burn," from His saying: *wa-taṣliyatu jaḥīm* (Verse 94, Surat al-Waqiʿah). The second reading comes from *al-ʾiṣlāʾ* (causing to burn), meaning "Allah will cause him to burn," from His saying: *fa-sawfa nuṣlīhi nāran* (Verse 30, Surat al-Nisaʾ).

The first reading is the preferred one (al-ikhtiyar), because the people (of recitation) have agreed upon it (li-ijmaʿ al-nās ʿalayhā). It derives from His saying: *illā man huwa ṣālī al-jaḥīm* (Verse 163, Surat al-Saffat).

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 111, verse 4:**

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and his wife, Umm Jamil﴾. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "al-'Awra'" means "Umm Qabih," and she was one-eyed (a'war). ﴿The carrier of firewood﴾[[(Recited with a raised ending (al-raf') by Nafi', and the author (al-Qurtubi) also recites it this way.)]]. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: she used to walk about among people spreading tale-bearing (namimah). The Arabs say, "So-and-so carries firewood against so-and-so" (yahtibu 'ala fulan) when he incites discord against him (idha warrash 'alayh).[[al-Tawrish: al-Tahrish (inciting discord). One says: "warrashtu bayna al-qawm" and "arrashtu."]] A poet said:

"The sons of al-Adram are the carriers of firewood,
They are the informers in contentment and in anger.
Upon them is the curse, continuous, and plunder."[[al-Harb (with a vowel on the 'ha' and 'ra' as in tahrik): the plundering of a person's property, leaving him with nothing.]]

Another said:

"Of the fair-skinned women, she did not hunt upon the back of the armor,
Nor did she walk among the tribe carrying green firewood."

He means: she did not walk about with tale-bearing, and he made the firewood "green" (ratb) to indicate smoking (tadkhin), which increases evil.

Aktham ibn Sayfi said to his sons: "Beware of tale-bearing! For it is a burning fire, and the tale-bearer accomplishes in an hour what the sorcerer does not accomplish in a month." One of the poets took this and said:

"Tale-bearing is a fire, woe to it, a burning one,
So flee from it and keep away from whoever practices it."

Therefore it is said: "The fire of resentment does not die down."

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A tale-bearer will not enter Paradise." And he said: "The two-faced one will not be considered honorable (wajih) with Allah." And peace and blessings be upon him said: "Among the worst of people is the two-faced one, who comes to these with one face and to those with another."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: The Children of Israel were struck by drought, so Musa (peace be upon him) brought them out three times to seek rain, but they were not given rain. Musa said: "My Lord, Your servants..." and Allah revealed to him: "I will not answer you, nor whoever is with you, because among them there is a man who is a tale-bearer, who persists in tale-bearing." Musa said: "O Lord, who is he, so that we may expel him from among us?" He said: "O Musa, I forbid you from tale-bearing, and shall I be a tale-bearer?" He said: So they all repented, and they were given rain.

Tale-bearing is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), there is no disagreement about this, to the extent that al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Three things destroy good deeds, nullify the fast of the fasting person, and break wudu': backbiting (ghibah), tale-bearing (namimah), and lying."

'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib said: I mentioned to al-Sha'bi the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Whoever sheds blood will not enter Paradise, nor will a tale-bearer, nor a merchant who practices usury (yurbi)." I said: "O Abu 'Amr, he joined the tale-bearer with the murderer and the consumer of usury?" He said: "Do blood get shed, and wealth get plundered, and great matters get stirred up, except because of tale-bearing?"

Qatadah and others said: She used to reproach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for poverty. Then, despite her abundant wealth, she would carry firewood on her back, due to her extreme stinginess, so she was reproached for miserliness.

Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: She used to carry thorny shrubs ('idah) and thorns (shawk), and would throw them at night on the path of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. al-Rabi' said: So the Prophet (ﷺ) would tread upon it as one treads upon silk.

Murrah al-Hamdani said: Umm Jamil would come every day with a large bundle (ibalah)[[al-Ibalah: a large bundle.]] of al-hasak,[[al-Hasak: a plant bearing a fruit with thorns that cling to sheep's wool and to al-sa'dan.]] and throw it on the path of the Muslims. One day, while she was carrying a bundle, she became exhausted, so she sat on a stone to rest, and the angel pulled her from behind and destroyed her.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The carrier of sins and offenses" (hammalat al-khataya wa al-dhunub), from their saying: "So-and-so carries firewood on his back" (yahtatibu 'ala dhahrihi). Its evidence is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And they carry their burdens upon their backs﴾.[[Verse 31, Surah al-An'am.]] [Al-An'am: 31]. It was also said: the meaning is "the carrier of firewood in the Fire," but this is far-fetched (fihi bu'd).

The reading of the majority (qira'at al-'amma) is "ḥammālatu" (حَمَّالَةُ) with a raised ending, so that it is a predicate (khabar) and "wa-imra'atuhu" is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). Then "fi jidiha hablun min masad" (فِي جِيدِهَا حَبْلٌ مِنْ مَسَدٍ) is a clause in the position of a circumstantial (hal) relating to the pronoun in "ḥammālah." Or it is a second predicate (khabar thani). Or "ḥammālatu al-ḥaṭab" (حَمَّالَةُ الْحَطَبِ) is an adjective (na't) for his wife, and the predicate is "fi jidiha hablun min masad," in which case one stops (yuwqaf) at "dhāta lahab" (ذاتَ لَهَبٍ) according to this view. It is also permissible that "wa-imra'atuhu" be conjoined (ma'tufah) to the pronoun in "sayaṣlā" (سَيَصْلى), so one does not stop at "dhāta lahab," and one stops at "wa-imra'atuhu," and "ḥammālatu al-ḥaṭab" is the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar ibtida' mahdhuf).

'Asim read "ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab" (حَمَّالَةَ الْحَطَبِ) in the accusative (naṣb) as a censure (dhamm), as if she had become known for this, so the adjective comes for censure and not for specification, like His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Cursed, wherever they are found﴾.[[Verse 61, Surah al-Ahzab.]] Abu Qilabah read "ḥāmilatu al-ḥaṭab" (حَامِلَةُ الْحَطَبِ).

Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 111, verse 5:

Allah's words, ﴿in her neck﴾, means: in her neck (*jid*, the neck).

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"A neck like the neck of a white gazelle, neither ugly*
*when she raises it, nor unadorned."* [[Al-jid: the neck. Al-rim: a white gazelle of pure whiteness. "Nassathu" means she raised it. Al-mu'attal: one with no ornaments on it. His words "bi-fahsh" mean it is not of unpleasant appearance.]]

﴿A rope of fiber﴾ means a rope of palm fiber (*masad*, fiber). Al-Nabigha said:

*"Thrown with flesh packed tight, its mature ones,*
*it has a creak like the creak of the pulley-wheel with the fiber."* [[Al-Tibrizi said: "Maqdhufa" means thrown with flesh. Al-dakhis means one whose parts have pressed into each other from its abundance. Al-nahdh is flesh, the plural of nahda. Al-bazil means the large one. Al-sarif is the creak. Al-qa'w is what holds the wheel together when it is wood; if it is iron, it is called khattaf. It is also narrated as "lahu sarif sarif al-qa'w" with a damma on the qa'w, and the accusative is better.]]

Another poet said:

*"O fiber of the palm-leaf fronds, protect yourself from me,*
*if you are supple and soft, for I*
*am as you wish, of a graying old man of full strength."* [[Al-ashmat: one whose white hair is mixed with black. Al-muqsi'nn: one who has reached the end of his age, so he has neither the weakness of old age nor the strength of youth. It is also said he is one in the last part of his youth and the first part of his old age. The verse is three lines in al-Lisan (under "masad"), and he did not attribute it to its speaker.]]

It may also be made of camel hides or camel hair. The poet said:

*"And a fiber twisted from she-camels,*
*not old-toothed and not four-year-olds."* [[Amara al-habl: he twisted the rope very tightly. Ayaniq: the plural of aynaq, and aynaq is the plural of naqa (she-camel). Al-anyab: the plural of nab, which is an aged she-camel. Al-haqa'iq: the plural of haqqa, one that has entered its fourth year and whose hide is not strong. The verse is three lines in al-Lisan. Al-Asma'i attributed it to Umara ibn Tariq. Abu Ubayda said it is by Uqba al-Hujaymi. His words "laysa" appear thus in al-Lisan (under "masad"), but he repeated it under "haqq" as "lasna" with the nun, and that is correct.]]

The plural of *jid* is *ajyad*, and the plural of *masad* is *amsad*.

Abu Ubayda said: it is a rope made of wool.

Al-Hasan said: they are ropes of a tree that grows in Yemen, called *masad*, and they used to be twisted.

Al-Dahhak and others said: this refers to the world. She used to taunt the Prophet (ﷺ) with poverty while she was gathering firewood, with a rope of fiber she put around her neck. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, strangled her with it and destroyed her. In the Hereafter, it is a rope of fire.

Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Abu Salih, said regarding ﴿in her neck a rope of fiber﴾: it is a chain whose length is seventy cubits.

Mujahid and Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said the same: it enters from her mouth and exits from her lower part, and the rest of it is wound around her neck.

Qatada said regarding ﴿a rope of fiber﴾: it is a necklace of *wada'* (cowrie shells). *Al-wada'* are white beads that come out of the sea, varying in size. The poet said:

*"And the wisdom is the wisdom of a child who sucks on the wada'."* [[Marra al-wada' yamruthuhu marthan: he sucked it.]]

The plural is *wada'at*.

Al-Hasan said: it was only a bead on her neck.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: she had a splendid necklace of jewels, and she said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will spend it in enmity toward Muhammad." And this will be a punishment on her neck on the Day of Resurrection.

It was also said that this is an indication of abandonment (*khidhlan*), meaning that she is bound away from faith by the misery that was decreed for her, like one bound at the neck with a rope of fiber.

*Al-masad* means twisting. It is said: "He twisted his rope, *yamsiduhu masdan*," meaning he twisted it well.

The poet (Ru'ba) said:

*"He twists the upper part of its flesh and binds it firmly."*

He means that the green fodder strengthens the back of this donkey and firms it up.

A creature described as *mamsuda al-khalq* is one with a very strong build. The poet said:

*"And a fiber twisted from she-camels,*
*of reddish, noble, fat-filled ones, whose marrow is abundant,*
*not weak-boned, and not old-toothed or four-year-olds."* [[Amara al-habl: he twisted it tightly. Al-ayaniq: the plural of naqa. Al-suhb: the plural of al-ashhab, a camel that is not very white. Ataq: the plural of atiq, meaning noble. Zahaq al-mukh: when its flesh is compact (gathered), so it is zahiq.]]

It is also narrated as:

*"Nor weak ones whose marrow is zahiq."*

Al-Farra' said: it is in the nominative, and the verse is *mukfa'* (a poem with mismatched case endings in its rhyme). He means: rather, its marrow is compact. He put it in the nominative as a starting sentence (*ibtida'*). He said: it is not permissible to mean "nor weak ones, zahiq is their marrow," just as one cannot say "I passed by a man whose father is standing" in the genitive.

Others said: *al-zahiq* here means *al-dhahib* (the departing one), as if he said: "nor weak ones, their marrow," and then he referred *al-zahiq* back to *al-dida'* (the weak ones).

A *rajul mamsud* means a man of firm build. A girl with a good *masad*, *'asab*, *jadal*, and *aram* (all terms for sturdy build), is *mamsudah*, *m'asubah*, *majdulah*, and *ma'rumah*.

*Al-misad*, with the pattern *fi'al*, is a dialectal variant of *al-misab*, which is a jar of ghee and a skin for honey. Al-Jawhari transmitted all of this.

It has been objected: if that was the rope she used for gathering firewood, how can it remain in the Fire? It was answered that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is able to renew it every time it burns.

The judgment that Abu Lahab and his wife remain in the Fire is conditional on their remaining in disbelief until their death (*al-muwafat*). [[Thus in the sources, and the word is apparently a corruption of "al-wafat" (death).]] When they died in disbelief, the report about them was proven true, and in this is a miracle of the Prophet (ﷺ). His wife was strangled by Allah with her rope, and Abu Lahab was struck by Allah with the *'adasa* (a plague-like pustule).

It happened seven nights after the battle of Badr, after Umm al-Fadl had struck him on the head. [[She was Lubaba al-Kubra bint al-Harith ibn Hazn al-Hilaliyya, sister of Maymuna, the Mother of the Believers.]] The reason was that when al-Haysuman came to Mecca to report the news of Badr, Abu Lahab said to him: "Tell me the news of the people." He said: "Yes, by Allah, when we met the people, we gave them our backs; they laid down their weapons among us wherever they wished. Even so, I did not blame the people. We met men, white, on piebald horses; by Allah, they left nothing of us." He meant: they left nothing of us at all.

Abu Rafi' said: I was a slave of al-Abbas, carving arrows in the house beside Zamzam. Umm al-Fadl was sitting with me, and what had come to us of the news had gladdened us. I lifted the tent-rope of the chamber and said: "By Allah, those are the angels!" Abu Lahab raised his hand and struck my face a severe blow. I attacked him (*thawartuhu*, meaning I lunged at him). [[Al-mathawara: the leaping upon. (Al-Lisan: "thawr".)]] I was a weak man, so he overpowered me, threw me to the ground, sat on my chest, and began beating me. Umm al-Fadl went for one of the pillars of the chamber, took it, and said: "You took advantage of him because his master was absent!" She struck him on the head with the pillar and split his head in a severe wound. He got up dragging his feet in humiliation. Allah struck him with the *'adasa*, and he died. He remained for three days without being buried until he stank. Then his sons washed him with water, pouring it on him from a distance, for fear of contagion from the *'adasa*. The Quraysh used to avoid it as one avoids the plague. Then they carried him to the upper part of Mecca, leaned him against a wall, and then piled stones on him, [[Raddamu: meaning they placed stones on top of one another.]] piling stones over him.
